article.headline: Corporate Profits Near Post-War Highs Signal an Equity Melt-Up
article.lede: A FRED chart tracking the corporate profit share of America's gross domestic income against the labor compensation share over seven decades forms the empirical backbone of a bullish equity call. The two series — profits near their post-World War II ceiling, workers' wages near a multi-decade floor — point, in the analyst's reading, to conditions ripe for a rapid melt-up in equity prices. The argument rests not on sentiment alone but on a macroeconomic accounting identity that links government deficits directly to corporate earnings.
article.body:
The FRED chart posted by @Globalflows tracks two competing claims on **gross domestic income** — the income-side measure of U.S. economic output — over seven decades. The left-axis series (corporate profits with *IVA* and *CCAdj*, as a fraction of GDI) and the right-axis series (compensation of employees as a fraction of GDI) together illustrate a long redistribution: workers' share has declined from roughly 58% in 1980 to about 51% today, while corporate profits have recovered from each recessionary trough to sit at approximately 11.5% of GDI in 2024 — near the top of the post-World War II historical range.

The mechanical underpinning of the melt-up argument is the *Kalecki-Levy profit equation*, a national-income accounting identity holding that aggregate corporate profits equal net investment plus dividends minus household saving minus government saving minus foreign saving. In practical terms: **large fiscal deficits flow directly into corporate earnings**. With the federal government running structural deficits well above peacetime norms, full-year 2025 domestic profit growth accelerated 49% over 2024 — $275.7 billion versus $184.4 billion — even as real GDI expanded only 2.4%. The profit share, in short, kept rising.

Labor compensation near its multi-decade floor creates maximum *operating leverage*: each incremental dollar of revenue flows disproportionately to shareholders rather than to wages. The *credit cycle* amplifies this. @Globalflows has noted that high-yield debt issuance has been running at record pace even with elevated credit spreads; if spreads compress, a further loosening of the borrowing spigot would, through the Kalecki mechanism, funnel more capital into investment and back into profits. He supplements this with an *impossible trinity* framework — the standard trilemma of independent monetary policy, open capital flows, and fixed exchange rates — arguing that the United States sits structurally at the center of every other nation's monetary constraint, and that dollar-recycling (foreign exporters earn dollars, buy Treasuries, suppress U.S. rates) provides a persistent bid under American equities regardless of domestic monetary settings.

The bear case is visible on the same chart. The *cyclically adjusted price-earnings ratio* (CAPE) stands around 35 times earnings on conventional figures and closer to 50 times when those earnings are adjusted for the elevated profit margin — levels that have historically preceded a decade of flat or negative real equity returns. The Kalecki equation also runs in reverse: fiscal consolidation, a rise in household savings, or a foreign buyers' strike on Treasuries would subtract directly from corporate earnings. Tariff escalations of early 2025 add input costs that were absent in 2021 — the last melt-up @Globalflows cites as his template. Whether the arithmetic sustains — profits high, labor cheap, credit expanding — or whether the chart's near-vertical right edge marks a ceiling rather than a launchpad is the dispute the chart frames but does not resolve.

concepts.definition: A rapid, self-reinforcing surge in equity prices driven by momentum and fear-of-missing-out rather than by improvements in underlying fundamentals. Melt-ups typically occur late in a bull market when underweight fund managers capitulate and chase performance, driving valuations well above historical norms before a sharp reversal. Jeremy Grantham's January 2018 letter popularized the term in modern financial commentary.

The income-side measure of U.S. economic output, equivalent in theory to GDP but measured from the opposite direction — by summing all income earned in production (wages, profits, interest, rent) rather than all spending. GDI and GDP should be identical but differ in practice due to measurement error. The BEA publishes shares of GDI for corporate profits, labor compensation, and other claimants separately.

An accounting adjustment applied to corporate profit figures that strips out gains or losses arising from changes in the price of inventories rather than changes in their volume. Without the IVA, reported profits are artificially inflated during periods of rising commodity or input prices, overstating the true economic profitability of production.

An adjustment that replaces tax-based depreciation — which depends on whatever Congress happens to allow — with economic depreciation based on the actual replacement cost of capital. Together with the IVA, it produces the clean profit figure used in national income accounting and plotted in the FRED series shown in this chart.

A macroeconomic accounting identity — derived independently by Polish economist Michal Kalecki and American economist Jerome Levy — showing that aggregate corporate profits equal net investment plus dividends minus household saving minus government saving minus foreign saving. The equation implies that fiscal deficits mechanically boost corporate earnings and that fiscal austerity or a rise in household saving mechanically compresses them. It is a sectoral-balances identity, not a forecast, so it is always exactly true by construction.

The fraction of national income paid to workers as wages, salaries, and benefits. The U.S. labor share of GDI has declined from roughly 58% in 1980 to about 51% today, driven by de-unionization, automation, and the rise of capital-light technology firms that generate high profits with relatively few employees. The decline is the mirror image of the rise in corporate profit share shown in the chart.

A stock market valuation metric developed by economist Robert Shiller that divides the current S&P 500 index level by the average of inflation-adjusted earnings over the prior ten years. By smoothing out the business cycle, CAPE reduces distortion from a single year of unusually high or low earnings. A CAPE above 30 has historically signaled below-average real equity returns over the subsequent decade.

A principle in international economics holding that a country cannot simultaneously maintain a fixed exchange rate, free capital flows, and an independent monetary policy — only two of the three are achievable at once. @Globalflows uses this framework to argue that U.S. dollar dominance puts America at the structural center of every other nation's monetary trade-off, creating a persistent recycling of foreign-earned dollars back into U.S. Treasuries and equities.

The recurring pattern of expansion and contraction in the availability and cost of credit across the economy. During the expansion phase, lending standards loosen, high-yield debt issuance rises, and investment accelerates — which feeds corporate profits through the Kalecki mechanism. Contraction phases reverse the flow, compressing profits and equity valuations.

The sensitivity of profits to changes in revenue, determined by the ratio of fixed costs to variable costs. When labor — a large variable cost — is a smaller share of revenues, companies have higher operating leverage: a given percentage increase in sales produces a proportionally larger increase in earnings, amplifying the link between economic growth and equity appreciation.

article.fact_check: The underlying data is sound: corporate profits with IVA and CCAdj stand near post-WWII highs as a share of GDI, and labor compensation is near multi-decade lows. The contested inference is 'just getting started.' A profit share already at approximately 11.5% of GDI sits near the historical ceiling of the 75-year range visible on the chart — not a midpoint — which makes mean-reversion risk non-trivial. The Kalecki equation is a reliable accounting identity, but the fiscal support it describes can reverse: any meaningful narrowing of the federal deficit would subtract directly from aggregate corporate earnings. The CAPE ratio at roughly 35 times earnings (or approximately 50 times on a margin-adjusted basis) is at levels that have historically produced flat or negative real equity returns over subsequent decades. None of this makes the melt-up thesis wrong — stretched valuations can extend further before correcting — but framing the current position as 'just getting started' understates how much of the profit-share expansion has already occurred.

poster_globalflows.blurb: Capital Flows (@Globalflows) is a self-identified Christian macro analyst who maps the macroeconomic regime across rates, FX, and equities to identify high-conviction trades. They post daily macro analysis, free reports, and educational threads covering topics like S&P 500 sector performance, factor analysis, and cross-asset correlations. They host a live weekday stream at 8:30am MST and share free daily reports with followers.
